contribution: The change of direction of the velocity in uniform circular motion is interpreted as an acceleration: the centripetal acceleration $a_\text{n} = \tfrac{v^2}{r}$ points to the centre, and Newton's second law gives a net force $m\tfrac{v^2}{r}$ towards the centre, which is the sum of the real forces (friction in a bend, tension in a string, the support force at a crest and in a dip); the centrifugal force is treated as a misconception, and the grip limit of a car is investigated with a simulation.
learn: recognise uniform circular motion and determine the direction and magnitude of the centripetal acceleration.
draw the free-body diagram of an object moving on a circular path and apply Newton's second law to it.
explain which force turns a car in a bend and where the feeling of being pressed outwards comes from.
prior: Tangential speed $v = \tfrac{2\pi r}{T}$ and the changing direction of the velocity in circular motion (chapter *Moving in a circle: period and speed*)
Drawing a free-body diagram and the equations of motion $\Sigma F_x = m a_x$ and $\Sigma F_y = m a_y$ (chapter *Free-body diagrams and the combined effect of forces*)
Static friction is at most $\mu_0 N$ (chapter *Weight, friction and the inclined plane*)

activities.text: On a slippery winter day a car comes into a bend a little too fast. The driver turns the steering wheel, but the car ends up in a snowbank. The passenger felt in the bend as if something pressed him outwards against the door.
activities.question: What force keeps a car in a bend, and is the force pressing outwards real?

activities.title: Review: velocity in circular motion
activities.prompt: An object goes round a circular path so that its tangential speed stays the same all the time. Which statement about its velocity $\overline{v}$ is true?

choices.text: The magnitude of the velocity stays the same, but its direction changes.
choices.feedback: Correct. As you learned in the chapter *Moving in a circle: period and speed*, the velocity is always along the tangent of the path, so its direction turns as the object goes round. This chapter finds out what the change of direction means for acceleration and forces.

choices.text: The velocity stays completely the same, because the speed of the object does not change.
choices.feedback: The speed, that is the magnitude of the velocity, stays the same, but velocity is a vector that also has a direction. On a circular path the direction is always along the tangent of the path, so it keeps changing.

choices.text: The velocity points all the time straight to the centre of the path.
choices.feedback: The velocity is along the tangent of the path, that is perpendicular to the radius. If the velocity pointed to the centre, the object would move towards the centre and not along the circle.

activities.title: Prediction 1: the speed doubles
activities.prompt: A car drives on a horizontal circular path. The driver doubles the speed but stays on the same path. How large a friction force must the road now give the car in the sideways direction for the car to stay on the path?

choices.text: Four times as large as before.
choices.feedback: Correct. The friction must give the car the centripetal acceleration, which grows with the square of the speed. In the values of the model, a $1500\,\text{kg}$ car on a radius of $50\,\text{m}$ needs a friction of $3.0\,\text{kN}$ at a speed of $10\,\text{m/s}$ and $12\,\text{kN}$ at $20\,\text{m/s}$. That is more than dry asphalt can give, $11.8\,\text{kN}$, so the car slides.

choices.text: Twice as large as before.
choices.feedback: The friction needed grows faster than the speed. For a faster car the velocity arrow is longer, so the same change of direction means a larger change of velocity. In addition, a faster car turns through the same angle in a shorter time, so the direction of its velocity changes faster. In the values of the model the friction needed grows from $3.0\,\text{kN}$ to $12\,\text{kN}$, that is fourfold, when the speed grows from $10\,\text{m/s}$ to $20\,\text{m/s}$.

choices.text: Equally large, because the path is the same.
choices.feedback: The path is the same, but a faster car turns faster, so the direction of its velocity changes faster. That takes a greater force. In the values of the model the friction needed grows from $3.0\,\text{kN}$ to $12\,\text{kN}$ when the speed doubles.

activities.title: Prediction 2: when the grip fails
activities.prompt: A car goes round a circular path so fast that the friction of the road is no longer enough. How does the car move after that, seen from above?

choices.text: The car still turns, but less than the path does, and drifts over the outer edge of the path.
choices.feedback: Correct. The friction still points towards the centre but is not enough to turn the car at the rate of the path. In the simulation the car turns less than the path, and goes straighter the greater the speed, and drifts over the outer edge. No force pushes it outwards.

choices.text: The car slides straight away from the centre, along the radius.
choices.feedback: Then a force pointing outwards should act on the car, but there is none: no object pushes the car out. In the simulation the car turns less than the path, and goes straighter the greater the speed, because the friction is not enough to turn it at the rate of the path.

choices.text: The car stays on the path, but its speed slows down.
choices.feedback: In a bend the friction points towards the centre, that is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does not slow the car down but turns it. When the friction is not enough, the car turns too little: in the simulation it turns less than the path, and goes straighter the greater the speed, and drifts over the outer edge of the path.

activities.title: Prediction 3: a light and a heavy car
activities.prompt: A light and a heavy car drive through the same bend at the same speed. The tyres and the road are similar. Which slides off the bend more easily?

choices.text: Neither slides more easily: the limit is the same.
choices.feedback: Correct. The heavy car needs a greater friction, $m\tfrac{v^2}{r}$, but it also presses on the road harder, so the maximum static friction $\mu_0 mg$ is greater in the same proportion. In the values of the model, at a speed of $19\,\text{m/s}$ the friction needed is $0.92$ times the maximum static friction for all three masses.

choices.text: The heavy car, because it needs a greater friction.
choices.feedback: The heavy car needs a greater friction, but it presses on the road with a greater force, so the road can also give it a greater friction. In the values of the model the ratio of the friction needed to the maximum friction is $0.92$ whatever the mass.

choices.text: The light car, because it presses on the road less.
choices.feedback: The light car gets a smaller friction, but it also needs a smaller one, because its mass is smaller. The mass cancels from the condition $m\tfrac{v^2}{r} \le \mu_0 mg$. In the values of the model the ratio is $0.92$ for all masses.

activities.text: A car goes round a horizontal circular path. On the left is the path seen from above, on the right the free-body diagram of the car seen from behind and a comparison of the friction needed with the maximum static friction.
activities.howto: Choose the tangential speed $v$ and the radius $r$ of the path with the sliders, and the *Mass* of the car and the *Surface* of the road. Press *Start* and the car starts to go round the path. If the friction needed is greater than the maximum static friction, the car starts to slide. *Reset* puts the car back on the path. The readings update at once, also when the car is standing still. *Animation speed* slows down or speeds up the animation without changing the readings.
activities.model: The values are model values calculated by the simulation. The road is horizontal, air resistance and rolling resistance are neglected, and the forces on the tyres are added together into one support force and one friction force. The coefficients of static friction are model values: dry asphalt $\mu_0 = 0.80$, wet asphalt $0.50$ and ice $0.10$. When the grip fails, in the model the road still gives its maximum friction $\mu_0 mg$ perpendicular to the velocity of the car, so the car turns less than the path. For clarity the car and the arrows are drawn larger than to scale, and the path is always the same size in the picture.
activities.calc: The centripetal acceleration is $a_\text{n} = \tfrac{v^2}{r}$, and the car stays on the path if the friction of the road gives the net force $m\tfrac{v^2}{r}$ towards the centre. In the vertical direction $N = mg$, and $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$. The maximum static friction is $\mu_0 N = \mu_0 mg$. If $m\tfrac{v^2}{r} \le \mu_0 mg$, the friction is $F_\mu = m\tfrac{v^2}{r}$; otherwise $F_\mu = \mu_0 mg$, and the car slides off the path.

activities.title: Experiment 1: the speed grows
activities.intro: Test predictions 1 and 2. The initial state chooses a radius of $50\,\text{m}$, a mass of $1500\,\text{kg}$ and dry asphalt. Change only the tangential speed $v$. Record a measurement at the speeds $5$, $10$, $15$ and $20\,\text{m/s}$. Finally set the speed to $25\,\text{m/s}$ and then to $30\,\text{m/s}$, press *Start* for each, and compare how the car moves.

question.prompt: According to the table, the grip is enough at a speed of $15\,\text{m/s}$ but not at $20\,\text{m/s}$. Calculate the greatest tangential speed at which the car can still stay on this path on dry asphalt.
hints: At the limit speed the friction needed is exactly equal to the maximum static friction. Which forces act on the car in the horizontal and the vertical direction?
In the vertical direction $N = mg$. In the horizontal direction $\mu_0 mg = m\dfrac{v^2}{r}$.
The mass cancels: $v = \sqrt{\mu_0 g r}$, where $\mu_0 = 0.80$ and $r = 50\,\text{m}$.

mistakes.feedback: You forgot the coefficient of static friction. The maximum static friction is $\mu_0 mg$, not $mg$, so $v = \sqrt{\mu_0 g r}$.
This is $v^2$. Take the square root as well: $v = \sqrt{\mu_0 g r}$.

question.solution:
**Given:** radius $r = 50\,\text{m}$, mass $m = 1500\,\text{kg}$, coefficient of static friction of dry asphalt $\mu_0 = 0.80$ (model value); $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$

**Find:** the greatest tangential speed $v$ in $\text{m/s}$

**Principle:** The car is in uniform circular motion, so by Newton's second law the net force is $m\tfrac{v^2}{r}$ towards the centre. The only horizontal force is the static friction of the road, which can be at most $\mu_0 N$. At the limit speed the friction is at its maximum.

**Force diagram:** The car seen from behind as a rectangle, the centre of the bend on the right, $x$ towards the centre and $y$ up. The weight $\overline{G}$ from the centre downwards, the support force $\overline{N}$ from the bottom face upwards and equally long, and the maximum static friction $\overline{F}_\mu$ from the corner of the bottom face towards the centre. The acceleration separately towards the centre.
```voimakuvio
pinta 0
G 14715
N 14715
F_mu 11772 oikea
a oikea
akselit 0
```

**Formula:** $y$: $N - mg = 0$ and $x$: $\mu_0 N = m\dfrac{v^2}{r}$, so $\mu_0 mg = m\dfrac{v^2}{r}$ and $v = \sqrt{\mu_0 g r}$

**Conversions:** The quantities are in SI units, so no conversions are needed, and the mass cancels.

**Substitution:** $v = \sqrt{0.80\cdot 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2\cdot 50\,\text{m}} = \sqrt{392.4\,\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2} = 19.81\,\text{m/s}$

**Answer:** $19.8\,\text{m/s}$ or about $71\,\text{km/h}$. The third figure is included because the limit is just below $20\,\text{m/s}$: the speed $20\,\text{m/s}$ in the table exceeds it.

**Reasonableness:** The result agrees with the table: at a speed of $15\,\text{m/s}$ the grip is enough and at $20\,\text{m/s}$ it is not. Check: at a speed of $19.8\,\text{m/s}$ the friction needed is $1500\,\text{kg}\cdot\tfrac{(19.8\,\text{m/s})^2}{50\,\text{m}} \approx 11.8\,\text{kN}$, the same as the maximum static friction.

activities.title: Experiment 2: the mass changes
activities.intro: Test prediction 3. The initial state chooses a radius of $50\,\text{m}$, dry asphalt and a speed of $19\,\text{m/s}$, which is close to the limit. Change only the mass and record a measurement at all three masses.

activities.title: Conclusion
activities.prompt: Using your measurements, explain how the friction needed depends on the speed, and why the car drifts over the outer edge of the path when the grip fails.
criteria: The answer says that double the speed requires four times the friction, and uses the numbers of the table.
The answer says that the car stays on the path only when the friction needed is at most the maximum static friction $\mu_0 mg$.
The answer says that the friction points towards the centre and that when the grip fails the car turns too little and no force pushes it out.
activities.model: In the table the friction needed grows with the square of the speed: at a speed of $10\,\text{m/s}$ it is $3.0\,\text{kN}$ and at $20\,\text{m/s}$ $12\,\text{kN}$, so double the speed requires four times the friction. In the values of the model the maximum static friction on dry asphalt is $11.8\,\text{kN}$. At a speed of $15\,\text{m/s}$ $6.75\,\text{kN}$ is needed and the grip is enough, but at $20\,\text{m/s}$ the friction needed is greater than the road can give. The friction points towards the centre and turns the car. When it is not enough, the car turns less than the path does, and goes straighter the greater the speed, and drifts over the outer edge of the path. A force pushing outwards is not needed to explain the motion.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the measurements and the theory. Also return to the passenger at the beginning: what force really acted on him in the bend, and in which direction did it point?

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt: A car drives at a steady speed over the top of a hill. A student drew the free-body diagram of the car as in the picture and named the force starting from the top face the centrifugal force $\overline{F}_\text{cf}$. What is wrong in the diagram?

choices.text: The force $\overline{F}_\text{cf}$ does not exist, and without it the sum of the forces points down.
choices.feedback: Correct. No object pulls the car upwards, so the centrifugal force is not drawn. At the top the car accelerates down towards the centre of the arc, so the sum of the forces cannot be zero: the weight is greater than the support force, $G - N = m\tfrac{v^2}{r}$.

choices.text: The support force should be as large as the weight.
choices.feedback: Then the sum of the forces would be zero, but at the top the car accelerates down towards the centre of the arc. The support force is rightly smaller than the weight. The error is the force $\overline{F}_\text{cf}$, which no object causes.

choices.text: The missing force is a centripetal force pointing down.
choices.feedback: The centripetal force is not a force of its own but the sum of the forces. Here it is the difference of the weight and the support force, so it is not drawn separately. The error is the force $\overline{F}_\text{cf}$, which no object causes.

choices.text: The weight should be smaller on the hill than on a level road.
choices.feedback: The weight $mg$ is the same on the hill and on a level road, because the gravitational pull of the Earth does not depend on the shape of the road. The support force changes. The error is the force $\overline{F}_\text{cf}$, which no object causes.

activities.title: Choose the right free-body diagram
activities.prompt: A car drives at a steady speed through the bottom of a dip. In which diagram is the free-body diagram of the car correct? Compare the arrows carefully: each wrong diagram has one error.

choices.feedback: Correct. At the bottom of the dip the centre of the arc is above, so the car accelerates up. So the support force is greater than the weight, $N - G = m\tfrac{v^2}{r}$, and the sum of the forces points up towards the centre.

Here the support force and the weight are equal, so the sum of the forces is zero. At the bottom of a dip, however, the car accelerates up towards the centre of the arc, so the support force must be greater than the weight.

Here the support force is smaller than the weight, so the sum of the forces points down. That is the case at the top of a hill. At the bottom of a dip the centre is above, so the support force must be greater than the weight.
Here there is also a force $\overline{F}_\text{cf}$ pointing down, which no object causes. Without it the diagram would be correct. The centrifugal force is not drawn in a free-body diagram.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: A roller-coaster car goes through the bottom of a dip at a steady speed. At the bottom the radius of the arc of the track is $12.0\,\text{m}$. At the bottom the seat presses the passenger with a force three times as large as his weight. How large is the speed of the car at the bottom of the dip?
hints: Draw the free-body diagram of the passenger. Which forces act on him in the vertical direction, and in which direction does he accelerate at the bottom of the dip?
The support force of the seat is $N = 3mg$. Choose $y$ up towards the centre of the arc: $N - mg = m\dfrac{v^2}{r}$.

mistakes.feedback: You forgot the weight. The net force is the difference of the support force and the weight: $N - mg = 3mg - mg = 2mg$, not $3mg$.
The net force is $N - mg = 3mg - mg = 2mg$, not $mg$. Then $v^2 = 2gr$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** radius of the arc $r = 12.0\,\text{m}$, support force of the seat $N = 3G = 3mg$, steady speed; $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$

**Find:** the speed $v$ of the car in $\text{m/s}$

**Principle:** At the bottom of the dip the passenger is for a moment on a circular path whose centre is above. By Newton's second law the net force points up towards the centre and equals $m\tfrac{v^2}{r}$. In the vertical direction the weight and the support force of the seat act on the passenger.

**Force diagram:** The passenger as a rectangle on the seat, $y$ up. The weight $\overline{G}$ from the centre downwards and the support force $\overline{N}$ of the seat from the bottom face upwards, three times the length of the weight. The acceleration separately as a thin orange arrow up towards the centre of the arc.
```voimakuvio
pinta 0
G 100
N 300
a ylös
v oikea
akselit 0
```

**Formula:** $y$: $N - mg = m\dfrac{v^2}{r}$ and $N = 3mg$, so $2mg = m\dfrac{v^2}{r}$ and $v = \sqrt{2gr}$

**Conversions:** The quantities are in SI units, so no conversions are needed, and the mass cancels.

**Substitution:** $v = \sqrt{2\cdot 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2\cdot 12.0\,\text{m}} = \sqrt{235.44\,\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2} = 15.34\,\text{m/s}$

**Answer:** $15.3\,\text{m/s}$, three significant figures like the radius $12.0\,\text{m}$.

**Reasonableness:** $15.3\,\text{m/s}$ is about $55\,\text{km/h}$, a normal roller-coaster speed. The centripetal acceleration is $\tfrac{(15.3\,\text{m/s})^2}{12.0\,\text{m}} \approx 19.6\,\text{m/s}^2 = 2g$, and in addition the seat has to give the weight: $3mg$ altogether, as in the task.

activities.text: Practise further at three levels. In the force tasks, first draw the free-body diagram in your notebook and choose one axis towards the centre of the path.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: A child sits on a roundabout that turns steadily. In which direction does the sum of the forces on the child point?

choices.text: Towards the centre of the roundabout.
choices.feedback: Correct. The child is in uniform circular motion, so he has a centripetal acceleration towards the centre. By Newton's second law the sum of the forces points in the same direction.

choices.text: In the direction of the velocity of the child, so that the motion continues.
choices.feedback: Motion does not need a force in the direction of the velocity to continue. The speed is constant, so there is no acceleration along the velocity. The direction of the velocity changes, and that takes a sum of forces pointing to the centre.

choices.text: Away from the centre, because the child is pressed outwards.
choices.feedback: The body of the child tends to continue straight on, and that is why it feels as if he were pressed outwards. The seat and the support, however, push him inwards, and the sum of the forces points towards the centre.

choices.text: The sum is zero, because the speed does not change.
choices.feedback: The speed does not change, but the direction of the velocity does, so the child has an acceleration. Then the sum of the forces cannot be zero: it points towards the centre.

activities.title: 2. Calculating
activities.prompt: A child of mass $30\,\text{kg}$ sits on a roundabout $2.0\,\text{m}$ from the centre. The roundabout makes one revolution in $4.0\,\text{s}$. How large is the sum of the forces on the child?
hints: First calculate the tangential speed of the child from the period.

mistakes.feedback: You forgot to square the speed. The centripetal acceleration is $\tfrac{v^2}{r}$, not $\tfrac{v}{r}$.
This is the weight of the child. What is asked is the sum of the forces, which points towards the centre: $m\tfrac{v^2}{r}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** $m = 30\,\text{kg}$, $r = 2.0\,\text{m}$, period $T = 4.0\,\text{s}$

**Find:** the sum of the forces $\Sigma F$ in $\text{N}$

**Principle:** The roundabout turns steadily, so the child is in uniform circular motion. The tangential speed is found from the period, and by Newton's second law the sum of the forces is $m\tfrac{v^2}{r}$ towards the centre.

**Formula:** $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$ and $\Sigma F = m\dfrac{v^2}{r}$

**Conversions:** The quantities are in SI units, so no conversions are needed.

**Substitution:** $v = \dfrac{2\pi\cdot 2.0\,\text{m}}{4.0\,\text{s}} = 3.142\,\text{m/s}$ and $\Sigma F = 30\,\text{kg}\cdot\dfrac{(3.142\,\text{m/s})^2}{2.0\,\text{m}} = 148.0\,\text{N}$

**Answer:** $150\,\text{N}$ or $1.5 \cdot 10^{2}\,\text{N}$ towards the centre, two significant figures like the radius $2.0\,\text{m}$ and the period $4.0\,\text{s}$.

**Reasonableness:** The force is about half of the weight of the child, $294\,\text{N}$, because the centripetal acceleration $4.9\,\text{m/s}^2$ is about half of the free-fall acceleration. The seat and the support can give this force, but the child has to hold on.

activities.title: 3. Draw it yourself
activities.prompt: An ice hockey puck of mass $0.17\,\text{kg}$ is tied with a string to a peg fixed in the ice. The puck slides on the ice along a horizontal circle of radius $0.50\,\text{m}$ at a steady speed of $1.5\,\text{m/s}$. Friction and air resistance are neglected. Draw the free-body diagram of the puck seen from the side on paper: the puck as a rectangle and each force from its point of application. Write the equations of motion and calculate the tension of the string.

criteria.detail: The diagram shows only the puck, not the string, the peg or the ice with their forces.
Three forces: the weight, the support force of the ice and the tension of the string. No centrifugal force, no force in the direction of the velocity and no separate centripetal force.
The weight down, the support force up and the tension horizontally along the string towards the peg, that is towards the centre of the circle.
The weight from the centre, the support force from the bottom face and the tension from the point where the string is attached; each with its own symbol.
The support force as long as the weight, the tension a little under half the length of the weight; the acceleration, if it is drawn, separately beside the puck.
$y$: $N - mg = 0$ and $x$ towards the centre: $T = m\tfrac{v^2}{r} \approx 0.77\,\text{N}$.

activities.model: The Earth, the ice and the string act on the puck. The weight $\overline{G}$ points down from the centre, and the support force $\overline{N}$ of the ice up from the bottom face. The tension $\overline{T}$ of the string points along the string towards the peg, that is towards the centre of the circle. There are no other forces: there is no centrifugal force, and the centripetal force is not drawn separately, because here it is the tension itself. The puck is in uniform circular motion, so the net force points to the centre. When $x$ points towards the centre and $y$ up: $y$: $N - mg = 0$, so $N = 0.17\,\text{kg}\cdot 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2 \approx 1.7\,\text{N}$. $x$: $T = m\dfrac{v^2}{r} = 0.17\,\text{kg}\cdot\dfrac{(1.5\,\text{m/s})^2}{0.50\,\text{m}} \approx 0.77\,\text{N}$. The tension is under half of the weight.

activities.text: Finally three quick questions. Answer first yourself and open the answer only then.
